lines.L01: Two samples freeze — and one plateau sits lower. Why?
lines.L02: Dissolved particles lower the freezing point. That is what an osmometer measures.
lines.L03: A freezing-point osmometer: sample tubes, a thermistor probe, a cooling block, a stirring wire and a display.
lines.L04: The cooling block supercools the sample below its freezing point.
lines.L05: The stirring wire vibrates, and freezing starts.
lines.L06: Released heat lifts the temperature to a plateau: the freezing point.
lines.L07: More particles, a deeper depression — and from it, the osmolality.
lines.L08: Osmolality is per kilogram of water, in mOsm/kg; osmolarity is per litre of solution.
lines.L09: In LabGuide: Lab → Instruments and methods → Clinical biochemistry → Osmometer.
lines.L10: The same schematic and parts, plus specimens — each with its source.
lines.L11: Particles, air bubbles, evaporated or viscous samples, and high alcohol or acetone distort the reading.
lines.L12: And an uncleaned container carries the last sample into the next.
lines.L13: Lab → Calculators → Calculated osmolality: from sodium, glucose and urea.
lines.L14: Add the measured value, and it shows the osmolal gap.
lines.L15: Measured or calculated — know which number you read.
lines.L16: LabGuide — Lab → Instruments and methods → Osmometer.
